before: I used to think John’s experience was mostly a modern map due to starting from more confusion, even though I already knew from DN 1, MN 26, and MN 36 that the Buddha learned mind-unification meditations (jhānas, where the mind gathers into one) from teachers before Buddhism, so that kind of unity as an initial practice stage is actually not new at all. They mistook those states for enlightenment; he saw that they weren’t liberating by themselves, but were useful for stabilizing and purifying the mind before penetrative insight (vipassanā). And no, vipassanā doesn’t mean Goenka-style body-scanning as many now believe.

before: This distinction isn’t laid out explicitly in the suttas. AN 11.12 says a noble disciple can reach ease and joy through recollecting the Buddha, Dhamma, & Saṅgha – the community of realized disciples – or recollecting ethical conduct, generosity, or qualities shared with heavenly beings. Besides that ease and joy from recollection, I find that unification can also loosen physically: the binding that normally holds all my senses together as one solid experience does so a bit less. I’ll use percentages as a playful way of talking about how much of that binding has loosened up. Around 1%, a person can still do everything fine. Around 5%, they can hardly do anything. (And partial untying goes beyond that range too.)
after: This distinction isn’t laid out explicitly in the suttas. AN 11.12 describes a different route to ease and joy: a noble disciple can reach them through recollecting the Buddha, Dhamma, & Saṅgha – the community of realized disciples – or recollecting ethical conduct, generosity, or qualities shared with heavenly beings. Besides that ease and joy from recollection, I find that unification can also loosen physically: the binding that normally holds all my senses together as one solid experience does so a bit less. I’ll use percentages as a playful way of talking about how much of that binding has loosened up. Around 1%, a person can still do everything fine. Around 5%, they can hardly do anything. (And partial untying goes beyond that range too.)

before: Iti 44 also shows the limit of nibbāna while you’re alive: a living arahant still has preferences and still feels pleasure and pain, although they won’t be reborn again, since there’s no more craving for existence driving that. Yet outside the nibbāna meditation itself, that constructed functioning is still running, and can still feel pleasure and pain. That’s what I mean by “saṃsāric” in this article: the constructed functioning that’s capable of dukkha (suffering or unsatisfactoriness).

before: The standard isn’t the non-stop, 24/7 bliss that Soh claimed, which is false. In AN 11.12, a noble disciple can reach ease through recollection, so ease is something a disciple reaches through practice, not a permanent state they’re stuck in. Also, there’s this quote from the Buddha in MN 75 where he says that what normal people perceive as sensual pleasure, he feels as pain. So enlightenment isn’t a simple bliss switch.

before: Stream entry’s greatest prize is a “release date”: AN 3.88 allows at most seven more lives before final awakening. There is actually quite a lot of modern academic evidence for rebirth. But who’s going around getting reborn if no permanent self exists? Buddhists don’t imagine any permanent self-essence/soul moving between bodies. Rather, rebirth is seen as a causal process: there is a continuity (often called a “mind-stream”), but there is not a “thing” that’s moving from one life to the next. Craving and clinging lead to becoming, and becoming leads to birth. More like a driverless car. The later Buddhist philosopher Milindapañha compared rebirth to one lamp being used to lighting another.

before: For me, nibbāna was really like waking up from a dream, except that nobody woke up. Reasoning can make the dream doubtful. The event made doubt about the dream impossible to reverse.

before: It’s worth noting that Bāhiya was not just lucky to get enlightened so fast. Ud 1.10 shows his urgency and immediate understanding, while the later Bāhiya Apadāna says he had aspired and practiced toward that quick comprehension for a hundred thousand eons. Most people are not as ready as Bāhiya was, so don’t be surprised if you can’t leap from complex PTSD, self-hatred, or a chaotic life directly into complete liberation just because I told you a sound heard itself. The Buddha’s Noble Eightfold Path still needs to be followed, and I would mainly highlight the importance of ethical practice, loving-kindness, inner-child reparenting, healthy relationships, and a supportive practice community.
